title: CAP in an interview: the first question of your non-functional requirements
dek: The CAP theorem confuses many candidates, yet in an interview it boils down to one question you ask early: when the network splits your system in two, should it refuse requests it can't answer correctly, or answer with what it has? Your answer shapes the rest of the design. This article explains the three letters, why the real choice is only between two, and how to decide.

items: C: every read sees the latest write, as if there were one copy. A: every request to a working server gets an answer, maybe not the latest. P: the system keeps going when the network between its servers fails.
Networks do fail, so P isn't optional. CAP then comes down to one choice for the moments when the network is split: consistency (refuse or wait) or availability (answer, possibly with old data).

Ask: would it be a disaster if a user briefly saw out-of-date data? Yes: choose consistency (seat booking, stock, money). No: choose availability (profiles, menus, reviews). Most features are the second kind.
Consistency: all servers show the same data at the same time. Once a write has succeeded, every later read, from any server, returns it.
Availability: every request that reaches a server that is up gets a response, without a promise that the response holds the latest data.
Partition tolerance: the system keeps working when messages between its servers are lost or delayed, that is, when the network splits the servers into groups that can't talk to each other.

body.x: The classic statement is that a distributed system can have only two of the three. Note that the C here is not the C in ACID: in ACID, consistency means a transaction leaves the data obeying its rules (no negative stock, every order has a customer). CAP's consistency is about copies agreeing. Same word, different idea.

Any system with more than one server talks over a network, and networks fail: a cable is cut, a router reboots, a data centre loses its link. So partition tolerance is not something you can decline. The question CAP actually asks is narrower: while the network is split, do you keep answering (availability) or do you keep the data correct (consistency)? You can't have both during the split. When the network is healthy, you can have both.

Zotato runs servers in Mumbai and in Singapore for its Southeast Asian users. A restaurant owner in Mumbai renames their restaurant from 'Spice Route' to 'Masala House'. The change is written in Mumbai and copied to Singapore, and a user in Singapore opening the restaurant sees the new name.

body.cap: Normally a change made in Mumbai is copied to Singapore within a fraction of a second, and readers on both sides see the same name.

body.x: Then the link between Mumbai and Singapore goes down. The Singapore server can't tell whether the name has changed since it last heard from Mumbai. A user there opens the restaurant. Should Singapore:

items: refuse, with an error, because it can't be sure its copy is current (choosing consistency), or
show the name it has, which might be out of date (choosing availability)?

body.cap: With the link down, Singapore must choose: an error, to stay consistent, or the name it has, to stay available. For a restaurant's name, the old name is clearly better than an error.

body.x: Here the answer is easy: showing 'Spice Route' for a few more minutes is far better than an error page. A stale name harms nobody. That is the kind of judgement CAP asks you to make for each part of a system.
Some features must never show stale data, even if that means refusing requests during a split:

items: Seat booking: if one fan books seat 14 in block C for the final, and during a split another fan's server still shows it free and sells it too, two people turn up for one seat.
Stock: if one plate of the day's special is left and two servers each believe it is available, both customers are charged for one plate.
Money: a wallet balance, a payment or a trading order book shown out of date leads to spending money twice or trading at a wrong price.

body.cap: If each copy decides on its own, two riders can both accept the same order. Anything only one person may have needs one decision, and so consistency.

body.x: Most features can show slightly old data for a while, and should keep answering. The data catches up when the network recovers (eventual consistency), within seconds or minutes:

items: Profiles: if a user changes their photo, others seeing the old one for a few minutes is fine.
Content: a dish description or a match preview shown out of date for a moment harms nobody.
Listings and reviews: a restaurant's opening hours or rating a little behind is far better than no page at all.

body.x: The question to ask for each feature: 'Would it be a disaster if users briefly saw inconsistent data?' If yes, choose consistency. If not, choose availability.

body.cap: One question per feature: would briefly stale data be a disaster? Seats, stock and money say yes; profiles, menus and reviews say no.

body.x: Where it goes in the interview

A design interview usually starts by agreeing the functional requirements (what the system does) and then the non-functional ones (how well: scale, latency, availability, durability). CAP belongs at the start of the non-functional list, because it changes what you build: ask 'Does this system need consistency or availability when the network fails?', and if the answer differs by feature, say so. The articles 'Designing for consistency or for availability' and 'Consistency per feature' show how the answer shapes the design.

items: State CAP in one line: during a network split, choose consistency or availability.
Decide per feature with the 'would stale data be a disaster?' question, and say the answer out loud.
Don't recite 'pick two of three'; P is not optional.
